network.overall_strategy: Construct ten distinct candidate reaction sequences converging on racemic aspartate: cyanoacetylene-derived aminonitrile hydrolysis; three oxaloacetate reductive-amination implementations; pyridoxamine-mediated transamination; Bucherer–Bergs trapping and hydrolysis; glyoxylate–malonate–urea chemistry; fumarate ammoniation; maleate ammoniation; and a discharge-derived amino-acid inventory channel. These are alternative experimental or proposed settings, not one compatible reaction mixture or ten independent reaction mechanisms. Oxaloacetate, hydroxylamine, pyridoxamine and the supplied organic acids are explicit boundary feedstocks whose geochemical production is not established here. Methane–nitrogen discharge provides a candidate internal cyanoacetylene source, but its coupling to downstream chemistry remains unverified. Hydrogen for nickel catalysis is supplied independently from a reducing geological reservoir, not collected from the discharge. Conditions identified as proposed are testable implementation windows, not published optimized protocols. Neutral parent acids represent pH-dependent acid/base pools; the target therefore uses the formula of aspartic acid rather than asserting its protonation state in every environment. Proton and iron-ion entries provide explicit redox and charge bookkeeping, while detailed surface complexation and acid/base equilibria remain unresolved. A null environment_formed denotes an external boundary supply or formation in multiple environments. All branches are anoxic, no homochiral synthesis is assumed, and oxaloacetate decarboxylation is represented explicitly as a competing loss reaction. The network is complete within these declared boundaries, not a demonstrated selective synthesis from C1 feedstocks under one geochemical regime.

reactions.name: Discharge production of cyanoacetylene and hydrogen cyanide

conditions.temperature: 300-330 K bulk gas and collection reservoir; transient discharge plasma is much hotter
conditions.other: Anoxic CH4/N2 electrical discharge in a locally reducing plume. A proposed implementation screens 1-10% CH4 in N2 and quenches the gas into a separate cool water collector within approximately one minute. NH3 and H2S are excluded from the discharge zone and introduced, if needed, only downstream. Gas composition, collection efficiency and residence time are design parameters, not an established early-Earth protocol.

reactions.mechanism: Energy-driven radical chemistry forms nitriles from methane-derived carbon and activated nitrogen. This is an atom-balanceable inventory-level transformation, not an elementary reaction or a measured coproduct ratio.
reactions.reasoning: Cyanoacetylene production in methane/nitrogen discharges supports this precursor source (Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel, 1966). Its yield decreases when NH3 or H2S is included, making separation of precursor generation and aqueous capture chemically necessary (Shapiro, 1999). Useful dissolved concentrations and survival during collection are unresolved bottlenecks. The H2 coproduct is not routed to nickel amination: that pathway uses an independent geological H2 boundary supply.

reactions.name: Cyanoacetylene-derived formation of 2-aminosuccinonitrile

conditions.other: Slightly alkaline water, proposed pH 8.5-9.5. Initial screening concentrations: 1-10 mM cyanoacetylene, 10-100 mM total cyanide and 0.1-1 M total NH3/NH4+. Sample over minutes to several hours. Fresh cyanoacetylene is delivered directly from the collection zone rather than stored for days. A shaded or turbid microbasin limits uncontrolled photolysis despite strong regional UV.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia addition and imine formation, potentially involving equilibrating hydrated species, followed by cyanide capture gives the four-carbon alpha-aminodinitrile. Water participates in proton-transfer and hydration equilibria but is not consumed in the net transformation.
reactions.reasoning: The supplied report attributes a 25% aminonitrile yield to slightly alkaline cyanoacetylene/HCN/NH3 chemistry (Patel et al., 2015). Maleonitrile and a cyanohydrin compete strongly; 25% is a branch yield, not an overall aspartate yield. The proposed concentration and residence-time window must be validated rather than assumed to reproduce that result. Cu photoredox and sulfide are not added because they are unnecessary for this aspartate branch and can introduce competing chemistry.

reactions.name: Partial aminodinitrile hydrolysis through an asparagine branch

conditions.other: Proposed pH 1-2 in an HCl-acidified geothermal pool, with sampling over 6-72 hours. Acidification occurs only after aminonitrile formation, through contact with a distinct acidic water body. This is a branch through partially hydrolysed products, not a claim that pure asparagine can be isolated selectively under these conditions.

reactions.mechanism: Hydration and hydrolysis of the alpha nitrile to a carboxyl group, accompanied by hydration of the side-chain nitrile to an amide, gives asparagine and releases ammonia. Several elementary hydration steps are grouped in this node.
reactions.reasoning: Aspartate and asparagine formation from cyanoacetylene-derived chemistry is supported by Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966), while Patel et al. (2015) establish the aminodinitrile precursor. The supplied evidence does not establish selective accumulation of asparagine or conversion rates at 360-370 K. The explicit asparagine branch and lower-than-boiling hydrolysis schedule are therefore mechanistically justified but experimentally unquantified implementations.

reactions.name: Asparagine side-chain amide hydrolysis to aspartate

conditions.other: Continue in an anoxic, acidic geothermal pool at proposed pH 1-2, with a 1-7 day screening interval. Cool and dilute the hydrolysate after conversion rather than exposing aspartate to prolonged hotter vent conditions. Sulfide-rich processing is avoided because sulfur-mediated amino-acid degradation may compete.

reactions.mechanism: Acid-catalysed hydrolysis of the side-chain carboxamide releases ammonia and converts asparagine to aspartic acid.
reactions.reasoning: This ordinary amide hydrolysis provides the chemically required completion of the Asp/Asn nitrile branch (Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel, 1966; Patel et al., 2015). The supplied studies do not quantify its yield or duration in the proposed pool window, so no quantitative end-to-end yield is assigned. Possible loss of acidic amino acids during sulfide-rich processing is a reason to separate this episode from sulfidic discharge chemistry (Parker et al., 2011).

reactions.name: Oxaloacetate reductive amination on electroreduced iron sulfide
agents: Electroreduced mackinawite-derived FeS_PERM with an analytically confirmed Fe0-bearing fraction

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 bar for the proposed capture assay
conditions.catalyst: FeS_PERM reactive surface; its Fe0 fraction is a consumed reductant
conditions.other: Anoxic mineral interface, proposed initial pH 9-10, 1-10 mM freshly supplied oxaloacetate and 0.4-1 M total NH3/NH4+. Provide a quantified excess of reactive Fe0 electron equivalents. Sample during the first minute to hour to establish competition with decarboxylation. The electroreduced mineral is a supplied energetic boundary; spontaneous regeneration is not assumed. Proton entries represent buffered proton equivalents, and Fe2+ is the formal oxidation product before surface binding or precipitation.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia forms an imine or iminium-derived surface intermediate, which receives reducing equivalents from Fe0-bearing material. Iron oxidation is explicitly represented rather than treating the reductant as an indefinitely reusable catalyst.
reactions.reasoning: Kitadai et al. (2019) reported approximately 64% aspartate from supplied oxaloacetate using electroreduced FeS. That result supports the capture chemistry, not the proposed operating window or a complete vent synthesis from CO2. Malate formation competes, and oxaloacetate supply remains unresolved. Cooling and immediate capture are selected because oxaloacetate decays on an hours timescale even near room temperature (Wolfenden et al., 2011). The high ammonia requirement and supply of electroreduced material are explicit geochemical limitations.

reactions.name: Hydrogen-driven oxaloacetate reductive amination over supported nickel

conditions.other: Initial pH approximately 8. Proposed oxaloacetate-specific screen: 1-10 mM freshly supplied oxaloacetate and 100-150 mM total NH3/NH4+, with early-time sampling and an endpoint up to 72 hours. The study investigated a broader 6-150 mM ammonium range, but the low-ammonia pyruvate result is not assigned to oxaloacetate. H2 comes from an independently pressurized geological reservoir. Cyanide and free sulfide are excluded from this catalyst compartment because they can poison nickel.

reactions.mechanism: Nickel activates molecular hydrogen and reduces the imine formed from oxaloacetate and ammonia. Direct carbonyl hydrogenation to malate competes with amination.
reactions.reasoning: Kaur et al. (2024) support H2-driven ketoacid amination at 295 K, pH 8 and 5 bar H2 over supported nickel. Crucially, their mixed oxaloacetate/glyoxylate network gave only trace aspartate with Ni; the approximately 5% mixed-network result belonged to Pd. No high Ni-aspartate yield is assumed here. The manufactured support is an experimental analogue, not proof that every natural Ni-bearing mineral performs equivalently. A 72-hour assay also does not imply that unreacted oxaloacetate survives for 72 hours.

reactions.name: Hydroxylamine-assisted reductive amination of oxaloacetate with iron
agents: Freshly exposed Fe0 surface; stoichiometric reductant

conditions.other: Separate acidic processing episode, initially approximately 1 M HCl. Proposed 1-10 mM supplied oxaloacetate and 10-100 mM hydroxylamine, with sufficient Fe0 for the four-electron reduction and additional allowance for competing corrosion. Sample over 1 minute to 4 hours. This acidic Fe0/NH2OH mixture is not combined with the alkaline FeS, nickel or Fe2+-promoted precursor-forming mixtures.

reactions.mechanism: Hydroxylamine condenses with the keto group to form an oxime. Reduction of the C=N and N-O functionality by iron-derived electrons gives aspartate, with water formation and Fe0 oxidation to Fe2+.
reactions.reasoning: Aspartate production following addition of hydroxylamine and Fe0 to an iron-promoted ketoacid network is supported by Muchowska et al. (2019). In that network, oxaloacetate was inferred from trapping products rather than directly quantified. The supplied report also identifies strong-acid Fe0 protocols and their incompatibility with other precursor-forming conditions (Kitadai et al., 2019; Kaur et al., 2024). The exact proposed capture schedule and an isolated-oxaloacetate yield are not established. Hydroxylamine availability is an unresolved boundary requirement.

reactions.name: Copper-assisted amino transfer from pyridoxamine to oxaloacetate
agents: Dissolved Cu2+ complexed by the reaction substrates

conditions.other: 10 mM oxaloacetate, 10 mM pyridoxamine and 50 mM NH4HCO3, initial pH 7.8. Sample at approximately 1 hour and 24 hours. Use a sulfide-poor, anoxic mineral-water compartment where Cu remains available rather than precipitating as sulfide. Regional Fe2+ abundance is not assumed to provide the required Cu chemistry. Pyridoxamine is a stoichiometric donor, not a catalyst regenerated elsewhere in this network.

reactions.mechanism: Metal-assisted Schiff-base formation and proton rearrangement transfer the amino group from pyridoxamine to oxaloacetate. Hydrolysis releases aspartate and pyridoxal without an external oxidant.
reactions.reasoning: Harrison et al. (2023) reported approximately 3.45% aspartate after 24 hours with Cu2+ and approximately 3-5% at early sampling, versus only approximately 0.026% without added metal. These measurements justify specifying Cu2+, concentrations and residence times rather than implying efficient uncatalysed transamination. Oxaloacetate decarboxylation remains competitive. The geochemical origin of stoichiometric pyridoxamine and maintenance of soluble Cu in an anoxic, commonly sulfidic world are unresolved.

reactions.name: Bucherer–Bergs capture of oxaloacetate as an aspartate-equivalent hydantoin

conditions.pressure: Approximately 1 bar in a covered aqueous compartment
conditions.other: Ammonia/carbonate-containing cyanide solution. Proposed initial pH 8-9, 1-10 mM freshly supplied oxaloacetate, 10-100 mM total cyanide and 0.1-0.5 M ammonium carbonate equivalents. Sample over the first hour and subsequently up to 24 hours; the detailed concentrations and residence time are proposed rather than extracted from the report. Heat only after trapping. Keep this compartment separate from cyanide-sensitive nickel and iron-metal processing.

reactions.mechanism: A lumped Bucherer–Bergs sequence combines cyanide addition, nitrogen incorporation, carbamate chemistry, ring closure and decarboxylation to produce the aspartate-equivalent hydantoin. CO2 appears on both sides because carbonate incorporation and carboxyl-group loss are included in the same node; it is not a claim of simple aldehyde Strecker chemistry.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) reported an approximately 69% oxaloacetate-derived hydantoin yield at room temperature and subsequent approximately 68% aspartate yield after heated conversion. Trapping the fragile ketoacid is well motivated, but its rate under the proposed concentrations must be measured against decarboxylation. The route requires cyanide and freshly available oxaloacetate in the same compartment, combining rather than resolving their supply problems.

reactions.name: Hydantoin ring opening to N-carbamoylaspartate

conditions.other: Warm the hydantoin-containing aqueous fraction only after the room-temperature trapping episode. Retain the ammonia/carbonate medium; proposed initial pH 8-10 and a 6-72 hour sampling series require validation because the supplied report does not give a complete time/pH protocol. No mineral catalyst or molecular oxygen is required.

reactions.mechanism: Water opens the hydantoin ring to give the acyclic ureido dicarboxylic acid N-carbamoylaspartate.
reactions.reasoning: The hydantoin-to-N-carbamoylaspartate-to-aspartate sequence is supported by Pulletikurti et al. (2022). The 353 K conversion stage is supported by the supplied report, whereas the detailed proposed pH and sampling schedule are not claimed as its optimized protocol. This staging avoids heating free oxaloacetate before it has been trapped. The approximately 68% literature figure applies to the reported aspartate outcome, not to an independently measured yield for this individual node.

reactions.name: Hydrolytic removal of the N-carbamoyl group

conditions.other: Continue aqueous geothermal cycling after ring opening, using the same ammonia/carbonate medium. Proposed initial pH 8-10 and sampling over 6-72 hours are implementation parameters, not a verified independent-step protocol. Quantify both free aspartate and cyclized ureido products before assigning conversion.

reactions.mechanism: Hydrolysis of the ureido functionality releases aspartate, ammonia and carbon dioxide. Cyclization toward dihydroorotate is a competing fate rather than an additional source of free aspartate assumed here.
reactions.reasoning: Pulletikurti et al. (2022) identify N-carbamoylaspartate in the hydantoin-derived route and report approximately 68% aspartate after the heated conversion sequence. The reported association with dihydroorotate formation requires measuring partitioning rather than treating all trapped carbon as aspartate. No separately established yield or rate for this node is available in the supplied summary.

reactions.name: Glyoxylate–malonate–urea condensation with hydrolytic aspartate release

conditions.temperature: Proposed staged operation: 300-323 K condensation, followed by a 353 K hydrolysis screen
conditions.other: Proposed initial pH 7.5-9.5, 10 mM glyoxylate, 10-100 mM malonate and 0.1-1 M urea. Follow the condensation for 24-72 hours, then test heated product release while measuring aspartate, retained carbamoyl species and dihydroorotate separately. These concentrations and the staged schedule are proposed because the supplied report does not specify a complete protocol for this particular substrate combination.

reactions.mechanism: An overall multistep node encompasses urea-associated carbonyl condensation, malonate-derived C-C bond formation, decarboxylation and hydrolytic nitrogen deprotection. Carbamoyl intermediates are mechanistically plausible, but no specific isolated intermediate is asserted for this substrate mixture. The net product set is balanceable with two CO2 molecules per aspartate.
reactions.reasoning: Aspartate and dihydroorotate production from glyoxylate, malonate and urea is attributed to Pulletikurti et al. (2022). This supports the endpoint transformation, not an independently verified intermediate sequence or the proposed operating schedule. Consequently, the mechanistic assignment and geochemical implementation remain partly speculative. The approximately 68% oxaloacetate-route yield must not be transferred to this branch. All three organic substrates remain explicit boundary supplies.

reactions.name: Candidate ammonia addition to fumarate

conditions.pressure: Confined aqueous system, approximately 10-100 bar to retain water and ammonia
conditions.other: Proposed 10-100 mM fumarate and 1-5 M total NH3/NH4+, initial room-temperature pH approximately 9-11, with 6-48 hour sampling. These high ammonia activities require an exceptional concentrated reservoir rather than a dilute open-ocean vent. No enzyme is present and no useful low-temperature conversion is assumed.

reactions.mechanism: Uncatalysed aza-Michael addition of ammonia across the fumarate double bond, followed by proton transfer, would give racemic aspartate.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative as a prebiotic operating pathway. The supplied fumarate-specific historical evidence is not adequately verified, and useful conversion at plausible geological ammonia concentrations is unknown. Heated maleate ammoniation provides a process analogy, not a measured fumarate yield (US5756839A, 1998). Metal-promoted networks support fumarate availability more generally (Muchowska et al., 2017, 2019). Fumarate avoids oxaloacetate decarboxylation, but its dianion is a challenging electrophile and its amination kinetics remain a research gap.

reactions.name: Thermal ammonia addition to maleate

conditions.pressure: Autogenous pressure in a confined aqueous reservoir, nominally 10-100 bar
conditions.other: Ammonium maleate with excess ammonia. A proposed geological analogue uses 10-100 mM maleate, 1-5 M total NH3/NH4+ and a 6-48 hour residence-time screen. Initial room-temperature pH is approximately 9-11. Temperature is process-supported; these particular concentrations, pressure range and residence times are proposed tests, not an established natural occurrence.

reactions.mechanism: Ammonia adds across the activated maleate double bond, with proton transfers yielding racemic aspartate. Maleate/fumarate interconversion and other thermal reactions can compete.
reactions.reasoning: Industrial patent literature establishes DL-aspartate formation from heated ammonium maleate with excess NH3, including the approximately 110-145 degrees C range summarized in the supplied report (US5756839A, 1998, and processes cited therein). This is stronger direct process evidence than the fumarate case, but it is not peer-reviewed proof of prebiotic performance. Geological implementation remains speculative because concentrated ammonia retention, substrate supply and selectivity under mineral-rich conditions are unverified.

reactions.name: Discharge-derived aspartate inventory after aqueous processing

conditions.temperature: 300-370 K bulk gas-water circulation; discharge plasma is transiently much hotter
conditions.other: Anoxic CH4/NH3-rich local plume or gas-water discharge analogue, with optional background H2. Proposed operation uses approximately week-long discharge exposure and repeated aqueous condensation. Reported inventory identifications can include hydrolytic workup. A geological substitute at no more than 370 K, proposed pH 1-2 for several days, must be validated rather than assumed equivalent to laboratory workup. This is separate from the NH3-free cyanoacetylene-generation compartment.

reactions.mechanism: Discharge produces mixed nitriles, carbonyl compounds and other organic precursors. Subsequent aqueous reactions and hydrolysis release a small aspartate fraction. The node is a formal, atom-balanceable overall inventory channel; its H2 output is not a measured stoichiometric coproduct yield, and numerous competing products are outside this target-directed graph.
reactions.reasoning: Aspartate-containing discharge inventories are supported by the Miller experiments and later reanalyses (Miller, 1953; Johnson et al., 2008; Parker et al., 2011). The initial 1953 assignment was tentative, and methane-discharge aspartate selectivity is only roughly 0.006-0.01 relative to glycine on a molar basis in the supplied compilation. This is a minor inventory source, not a selective primary route. Its microscopic chemistry may overlap the explicit nitrile branch, while the reducing atmosphere and natural analogue of analytical hydrolysis remain contested.

reactions.name: Competing oxaloacetate decarboxylation

conditions.other: pH 6.8 reference condition, with an uncatalysed rate constant approximately 2.8e-5 s^-1 and half-life approximately 6.9 hours. This is a benchmark, not the rate at every pathway pH. Higher temperatures and certain divalent metal ions accelerate loss. Pyruvate is a competing sink and is not silently recarboxylated to regenerate oxaloacetate.

reactions.mechanism: Beta-ketoacid decarboxylation releases CO2 and an enol-derived product that tautomerizes to pyruvate.
reactions.reasoning: Wolfenden et al. (2011) provide the room-temperature kinetic benchmark. It makes rapid capture, short transport times and early-time sampling essential for all oxaloacetate pathways. Hydrothermal CO2/H2 chemistry has produced pyruvate but has not established its carboxylation to oxaloacetate under the same conditions (Preiner et al., 2020). Therefore this graph includes the demonstrated loss reaction without inventing a compensating oxaloacetate-production step.

pathways.name: Discharge-fed cyanoacetylene and aminonitrile hydrolysis
pathways.description: Methane/nitrogen discharge supplies nitriles, followed by separate alkaline ammonia capture and acidic hydrolysis through an asparagine branch. Each chemistry segment has supporting evidence, but collection, concentration and staged coupling are not demonstrated end-to-end. The reported 25% aminonitrile branch yield is not an aspartate yield.

pathways.name: Electroreduced iron-sulfide capture of supplied oxaloacetate
pathways.description: Supplied oxaloacetate and ammonia are reductively coupled using Fe0-bearing FeS_PERM. Approximately 64% literature aspartate formation supports the transformation, not the proposed cool-interface implementation or upstream oxaloacetate synthesis.

pathways.name: Hydrogen and supported-nickel amination of supplied oxaloacetate
pathways.description: Independent geological H2 and supported Ni reduce an oxaloacetate/ammonia-derived imine. This is a different reductant/catalyst implementation of the same broad reaction family as P2. Mixed-network Ni experiments gave only trace aspartate, so no high yield is assigned.

pathways.name: Hydroxylamine and sacrificial-iron capture
pathways.description: A separate acidic episode converts supplied oxaloacetate through oxime chemistry using hydroxylamine and Fe0. This pathway is not combined with alkaline precursor-forming chemistry, and hydroxylamine supply remains unresolved.

pathways.name: Copper-assisted stoichiometric pyridoxamine transamination
pathways.description: Pyridoxamine transfers nitrogen to supplied oxaloacetate, producing pyridoxal and approximately 3-5% aspartate under the cited Cu-assisted conditions. Neither prebiotic cofactor synthesis nor donor regeneration is supplied by this network.

pathways.name: Oxaloacetate hydantoin trapping and staged product release
pathways.description: Cyanide/ammonia/carbonate chemistry traps supplied oxaloacetate as a hydantoin before warming. Ring opening gives N-carbamoylaspartate, and further hydrolysis releases aspartate. The reported approximately 68% endpoint is specific to the literature sequence, not a prediction for all proposed conditions.

pathways.name: Glyoxylate–malonate–urea carbon-skeleton assembly
pathways.description: Three supplied small organic compounds undergo condensation, C-C bond formation, decarboxylation and hydrolytic release. The aspartate endpoint is literature-supported, but the proposed implementation and detailed intermediate sequence are not established by the supplied report.

pathways.name: Candidate fumarate ammoniation
pathways.description: Fumarate provides a more persistent four-carbon boundary substrate than oxaloacetate. Heated addition of concentrated ammonia is a testable candidate, not a demonstrated efficient prebiotic pathway.

pathways.name: Process-supported maleate ammoniation
pathways.description: Heated ammonium maleate with excess ammonia gives racemic aspartate in industrial chemistry. Transfer to a confined geological reservoir is conditional on substrate concentration, ammonia retention and measured selectivity. P8 and P9 are distinct substrate-entry pathways within the same reaction family.

pathways.name: Low-selectivity reducing-discharge inventory channel
pathways.description: A methane/ammonia gas-water discharge followed by aqueous processing supplies a minor aspartate inventory. This is an experimentally motivated aggregate pathway, not a claim of a tenth independent microscopic mechanism; some nitrile chemistry may overlap P1.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The transformations align with Sanchez, Ferris and Orgel (1966) and Patel et al. (2015), including the approximately 25% aminodinitrile branch. Keeping ammonia out of the methane–nitrogen discharge addresses part of the cyanoacetylene-supply critique. However, collection and delivery of surviving cyanoacetylene are unverified, and the reaction records do not specify the alkaline capture conditions or subsequent hydrolysis conditions. An asparagine intermediate is plausible, but its accumulation and hydrolysis selectivity require evidence. All four reactions pass the supplied conservation check.
suggestions: Specify discharge composition, collection efficiency, residence time and gas-to-liquid trapping conditions; measure cyanoacetylene survival before aminonitrile formation.
Provide separate capture and hydrolysis protocols, with measured aminodinitrile, asparagine and aspartate yields rather than assuming selective sequential conversion.
Represent the major competing capture products when estimating target flux.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is among the strongest experimentally supported target-forming branches: Kitadai et al. (2019) reported approximately 64% aspartate using electroreduced, Fe0-bearing FeS. The supplied Fe/H+ balance correctly accounts for a two-electron reduction. The principal gap is implementation: the active FeS phase, electroreduction potential, preparation history, reagent concentrations and reaction conditions are unspecified. The rxn_016 score evaluates the validity of the competing oxaloacetate decay reaction, not its contribution to target synthesis.
suggestions: Specify FeS phase composition, accessible Fe0 loading, activation potential, energy source, pH, temperature and ammonia concentration.
Measure aspartate formation against oxaloacetate decarboxylation and reduction to malate under the same conditions.
Assign environment-specific kinetics to rxn_016; including a loss edge alone does not establish successful capture.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Hydrogen-driven reductive amination over supported nickel is chemically credible and supported by Kaur et al. (2024). Supplying hydrogen independently is consistent with the declared boundaries. Aspartate-specific performance nevertheless needs qualification: the reported trace yield with Ni concerned the OAA–glyoxylate network and should not be treated as either a universal isolated-OAA yield or evidence for efficient capture. Catalyst identity, pressure, pH and competing hydroxy-acid formation remain unspecified.
suggestions: Specify nickel oxidation state, support, loading, hydrogen pressure, pH, temperature and reaction duration; distinguish laboratory catalyst supply from a proposed natural analogue.
Measure isolated-OAA conversion and aspartate selectivity without importing yields from other ketoacids, Pd experiments or mixed-substrate experiments.
Use the reported 22 °C, pH 8 and 5 bar H2 conditions as a literature benchmark, not as conditions already established for this network.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Oxime formation followed by iron-mediated reduction is plausible and consistent with the hydroxylamine/Fe0 chemistry reported by Muchowska et al. (2019). The inferred two Fe atoms and four protons correctly provide four-electron bookkeeping. Treating hydroxylamine as an external feedstock and this branch as a separate implementation is appropriate. The missing experimental window prevents assessment of oxime capture, iron corrosion and oxaloacetate loss under the actual proposed conditions.
suggestions: Specify oxime-formation and reduction conditions, including any acidification, order of addition, Fe loading and residence time.
Resolve or experimentally verify the oxime intermediate and quantify competing hydroxylamine consumption and oxaloacetate decarboxylation.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The stoichiometric pyridoxamine-to-pyridoxal transformation is correctly represented and experimentally supported. Harrison et al. (2023) reported approximately 3–5% aspartate with Cu2+, alongside substantial competing chemistry. No cofactor-regeneration step is required for the explicitly stoichiometric boundary-defined route. The Surface label does not establish copper availability, speciation or the pH and temperature needed to reproduce the experiment.
suggestions: Specify Cu2+ concentration, buffer, pH, temperature and reaction duration, using the reported pH 7.8 and 70 °C experiment as a benchmark.
Quantify pyridoxal production and nitrogen transfer together with aspartate, pyruvate and alanine.
Justify copper availability and speciation in the selected anoxic setting without assuming that anoxia alone either supplies or excludes Cu2+.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This is a strongly supported capture-and-release strategy. Pulletikurti et al. (2022) reported approximately 69% hydantoin and 68% aspartate through N-carbamoylaspartate. The listed formulas and net reactions pass the conservation check; CO2 appearing on both sides of rxn_009 is not a balance violation. The staged release conditions remain unspecified. Additionally, mol_005 is an internal intermediate, so this pathway depends on HCN delivery from rxn_001 unless an external supply is explicitly added.
suggestions: Specify cyanide and ammonia/carbonate concentrations, trapping conditions, and separate ring-opening and decarbamoylation conditions, including the literature-supported heated release stage.
Provide the structure of mol_018 as the saturated aspartate-equivalent hydantoin and clarify carbonate incorporation and decarboxylation hidden by the net equation.
Document HCN collection and transfer, and quantify competing dihydroorotate formation and incomplete product release.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The glyoxylate–malonate–urea route aligns with the supplied Pulletikurti et al. research, which reports aspartate and dihydroorotate. The equation is balanced with two CO2 products and is acceptable as a lumped condensation, decarboxylation and hydrolysis sequence. It does not, by itself, establish the conditions or efficiency of free-aspartate release. The reaction record lacks the intermediate assignments and staged protocol needed to distinguish target production from accumulation of carbamoylated or cyclic products.
suggestions: Resolve the carbon-skeleton assembly and product-release stages, using mol_019 where experimentally supported.
Specify concentrations, pH, temperature and workup, and distinguish free aspartate from material detected only after hydrolysis.
Measure competing dihydroorotate production and cite the supporting experimental protocol directly.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Ammonia addition to fumarate is atom-balanced and gives the correct target connectivity, but useful uncatalysed conversion under the stated, unspecified hydrothermal setting is not established. The supplied research identifies sparse historical evidence rather than a verified prebiotic protocol. Enzymatic reversibility does not establish an adequate nonenzymatic rate, and carboxylate speciation can strongly affect alkene reactivity. Labeling this branch as a candidate appropriately communicates uncertainty but does not validate target production.
suggestions: Obtain a verified primary experimental source or test fumarate ammoniation across defined temperature, pH, ammonia concentration and pressure ranges.
Measure aspartate formation, substrate recovery, competing products and target degradation with a carbon and nitrogen balance.
Retain this as an exploratory branch rather than assigning it demonstrated productive flux.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Thermal conversion of ammonium maleate to racemic aspartate has process-literature support, including the patent literature summarized in US5756839A. The net addition is chemically valid. However, the demonstrated process uses approximately 110–145 °C, excess ammonia and pressure; the Hydrothermal label alone does not establish those concentrations, ammonia retention or residence times. Industrial feasibility therefore supports the transformation more strongly than the proposed environmental implementation.
suggestions: Specify temperature, pressure, ammonium maleate concentration, ammonia excess and reaction duration against a cited process protocol.
Justify confinement and ammonia retention in the proposed setting and measure target stability under the same thermal conditions.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: A reducing-discharge inventory containing aspartate is supported by the Miller literature and later reanalyses, including Johnson et al. (2008). The reaction is acceptable as an explicitly coarse-grained inventory channel, not an elementary mechanism. Its balanced equation does not establish quantitative product ratios or a measured hydrogen yield. The network correctly acknowledges low selectivity, but gas proportions, collection conditions and aqueous processing are insufficiently specified to predict free-aspartate output.
suggestions: Specify discharge energy, gas proportions, pressure, water temperature, collection time and post-discharge processing.
Report absolute aspartate yields and analytical identification, distinguishing free aspartate from hydrolysis-released material.
Use this as a low-selectivity inventory source without treating the formal net stoichiometry as a measured product distribution.

evaluation.network_feedback: The complete network is structurally valid: its 26 molecule nodes and 16 reaction nodes are connected, molecule IDs are consistent, and internal intermediates are reachable from the declared boundary inputs. The deterministic check establishes 10 reactions balanced as written and six balanceable with modest coefficients, with no conservation violations. Those coefficients should be encoded explicitly. Boundary feedstocks, independent hydrogen supply, alternative settings and racemic products are acceptable within the stated scope; no C1-to-target closure is required. Several branches genuinely support aspartate production, with P2 and P6 having particularly strong experimental backing. The main limitation is environmental and operational specification: despite references to proposed implementation windows, the reaction records provide no quantitative temperature, pressure, pH, concentration or residence-time windows. The Biochemical label is not itself a physicochemical environment, and catalyst preparation, availability and relevant transfers remain incompletely specified. Oxaloacetate decay is correctly included as rxn_016, but productive capture requires environment-specific kinetic competition. Literature alignment is good at the route-family level, and important limitations are acknowledged, but reaction-level citations and protocol mappings are absent. Fumarate ammoniation remains substantially less established than the demonstrated branches. Flagged reactions primarily have evidence or implementation gaps, not conservation failures. Overall, this is a credible, conditionally target-producing candidate network, but not yet sufficiently specified and validated to meet the 0.90 network-approval threshold.
